q: What is knowledge management?
r: Capturing, sharing and using what an organization knows
It helps people find and reuse information.
w: Keeping information secret from every employee in the firm
Deleting old documents to free up storage space only
Buying new computers for the whole office each year

q: What is explicit knowledge?
r: Knowledge that can be written down or recorded
Manuals and reports are examples.
w: Knowledge that people hold in their heads from experience
Knowledge that no one in the company can explain
Knowledge that is protected by a patent

q: What is tacit knowledge?
r: Knowledge gained from experience that is hard to write down
A skilled worker's know-how is an example.
w: Knowledge that is stored in a manual
Knowledge that is printed on a website
Knowledge that is shared in a company newsletter

q: A senior technician can fix machines by feel but has no written steps. Which type of knowledge is this?
r: Tacit knowledge
It lives in the person's experience.

q: What is a knowledge base?
r: A searchable collection of information that staff can use
It stores answers, guides and procedures.
w: A building where a firm stores its products
A group of experts who work on a project
A report that lists a firm's yearly profits

q: Why do companies document their processes?
r: So that others can follow them and the knowledge is not lost
Documentation preserves know-how.
w: So that no employee will ever need training
So that competitors can copy the whole business
So that the firm can avoid following any rules

q: A key employee is retiring. Which step best protects the company's knowledge?
r: Document key processes and pair the employee with a successor
Knowledge transfers before the person leaves.
w: Wait until the employee leaves, then ask what they did
Delete the employee's files on the last day
Hire someone who has never seen the work

q: What is a best practice?
r: A method shown to produce excellent results
Firms share them to improve performance.
w: A method used only once by one employee
A method that is cheapest regardless of results
Cost alone does not define it.
A method that is required by no one

q: What is an intranet?
r: A private network used inside an organization to share information
Employees use it to find documents.
w: A public website for customers to buy products
A social network used by teenagers
A device that stores backup tapes

q: What is a lesson learned?
r: Insight gained from a project that can improve future work
Teams record them after finishing.
w: A class that employees must attend each year
A rule that prevents mistakes in all cases
A report that lists employees' pay

q: After a failed product launch, a team writes down what went wrong. What is this practice?
r: Capturing lessons learned
It helps avoid repeating mistakes.
w: Hiding the failure from other teams
Blaming one employee for the result
Deleting all records of the launch

q: What is data?
r: Raw facts and figures
It needs processing to become useful.
w: Skill gained from years of work

q: What is information?
r: Data that has been organized and given meaning
It supports decisions.
w: A guess about the future with no evidence
A private opinion that has not been shared

q: A list shows 200, 220 and 250 for sales in three months. A manager notes sales are rising 10 percent a month. What did the manager create?
r: Information from data
The numbers were organized into a meaningful trend.
w: A secret that must not be shared
Information is meant to be used.

q: What is a cloud storage service used for?
r: Storing files online so they can be reached from many devices
It supports sharing and backup.
w: Making the weather more predictable for firms

q: Why should access to confidential files be limited?
r: To protect sensitive information from misuse
Only authorized staff should view it.
w: To make it harder for the owners to find files
To lower the cost of storage for the firm
To keep customers from ever paying

q: What is a community of practice?
r: A group of people who share a field and learn from each other
They exchange tips and solutions.
w: A group of customers who buy the same product
A group of suppliers who set prices together
That is not a learning group.
A group of rivals who hide information

q: What is mentoring?
r: Experienced employees guiding less experienced ones
It passes on know-how.
w: Managers firing employees who make mistakes
Customers training staff to sell products

q: Which is the best way to keep a company's knowledge current?
r: Review and update documents on a regular schedule
Old information can mislead.
w: Never change documents once they are written
Let each employee keep personal copies only
Delete any document older than a day

q: What is a database used for in knowledge management?
r: Storing organized information so it can be searched and updated
It supports quick access.
w: Printing posters for a store event

q: A support team often answers the same questions. Which tool best reduces the workload?
r: A searchable help center with common answers
Customers can find answers themselves.
w: A longer list of employee holidays
A new color for the company's logo
A bigger parking lot for staff

q: What is intellectual property?
r: Creations of the mind that are legally protected, such as inventions and brands
Patents and copyrights protect it.
w: Buildings and land owned by a company
Cash held in a company bank account

q: A company's secret recipe is a valuable asset. Which protection best keeps it confidential?
r: Trade secret protections such as limited access and confidentiality agreements
These keep the recipe private.
w: Publishing the recipe on the company website

q: What is an after-action review?
r: A discussion of what happened, why and how to improve
It turns experience into learning.
w: A report that lists the profits of a project
A party held after a project ends
A list of employees who left the project

q: What is onboarding's role in knowledge management?
r: Helping new employees quickly learn what the organization knows
It speeds up productivity.
w: Removing information from the company's files
Preventing new hires from asking questions

q: Which is a barrier to knowledge sharing?
r: Employees fear that sharing will reduce their value
Fear and poor culture block sharing.
w: Clear tools that make documents easy to find
Time set aside for teams to teach each other

q: What is a wiki used for in a company?
r: A shared site that staff can edit to build common knowledge
Many people can add and update pages.
w: A locked file that only one person can read
A tool for printing business cards

q: What is data security?
r: Protecting data from unauthorized access, loss or damage
Passwords and backups help.
w: Posting data publicly so everyone can see it
Deleting all data after it is used once

q: Which practice best protects company data on laptops?
r: Using strong passwords and encryption
They reduce the risk if a device is lost.
w: Writing passwords on sticky notes beside the screen
Leaving laptops unlocked in public places
Using the same password on every account

q: Why is it important to back up important files?
r: So they can be restored if the original is lost or damaged
Backups protect against loss.
w: So the files take up more space on purpose
So no one else can open the files
So the files can never be changed again

q: What is a standard operating procedure (SOP)?
r: A written set of steps for doing a task consistently
It reduces errors.
w: A schedule of when employees take breaks
A list of the products a firm sells
A report on a firm's quarterly results

q: A restaurant writes step-by-step instructions for opening each morning. What is this?
r: A standard operating procedure
It ensures the task is done the same way.
w: It is not a financial report.
A marketing plan for new customers
It is not a promotion plan.
A lease agreement for the building

q: What is quality?
r: How well a product or service meets customer needs
High quality satisfies customers.
w: How expensive a product is to produce
How many products a company sells
How large a product is when packaged

q: What is quality control?
r: Checking products or services to make sure they meet standards
It finds defects before delivery.
w: Raising the price of products that are high quality
Choosing which products to advertise this season
Setting production targets for next year

q: What is quality assurance?
r: Planned activities that prevent defects from happening
It focuses on the process.
w: Checking finished products for defects only at the end
Reducing the number of inspections to save money

q: Which is the best example of quality assurance rather than quality control?
r: Training workers on correct assembly steps before production begins
It prevents defects.
w: Inspecting finished items and removing broken ones
Counting the number of items rejected last week
Testing a sample of items after they are packed

q: What is a defect?
r: A flaw that makes a product fail to meet standards
Defects can lead to returns.
w: A price that is lower than rivals

q: What is total quality management (TQM)?
r: A company-wide approach to continuous improvement and customer satisfaction
Everyone shares responsibility for quality.
w: A method where only inspectors are responsible for quality
A method that ignores customer feedback
A method that focuses only on lowering prices

q: What is continuous improvement?
r: Making ongoing small changes that raise quality and efficiency
It never stops.
w: Making one large change and never changing again
Waiting for customers to complain before acting
Avoiding any change to existing methods

q: A factory team meets weekly to find small ways to reduce waste. Which idea does this show?
r: Continuous improvement
Small ongoing changes add up.
w: Market skimming for a new product

q: What is a quality standard?
r: A measure or rule a product must meet to be acceptable
Standards guide production.
w: A slogan that the company uses in ads
A discount offered to loyal customers

q: What is ISO 9001?
r: An international standard for quality management systems
Companies can be certified.
w: A tax form for international sales
That is not a quality standard.
A law that sets minimum wages
That is not a quality standard.
That is not a quality standard.

q: Why might a supplier seek ISO 9001 certification?
r: To show customers its processes meet recognized quality standards
Certification builds trust.
w: To avoid inspecting its own products ever again
To raise the price of every product automatically
To stop customers from comparing suppliers

q: What is Six Sigma?
r: A method that aims to reduce defects and variation in processes
It uses data to improve quality.
w: A method of hiring six new managers
A method of setting six prices for one product
A method of printing six copies of reports

q: What is benchmarking?
r: Comparing a firm's performance with the best in the industry
It reveals areas to improve.
w: Ignoring rivals to focus on internal data only
Setting the lowest possible goals for a team
Counting the benches in a company's lobby

q: A delivery company compares its on-time rate with the industry leader's. What is this?
r: Benchmarking
It measures against the best.

q: What is a customer complaint?
r: A statement that a product or service did not meet expectations
It is useful feedback.
w: A request to open a new account

q: What is the best way to treat customer complaints?
r: Treat them as feedback that can reveal quality problems
They show where to improve.
w: Ignore them so that staff stay positive
Blame the customer for every issue

q: What is a root cause?
r: The underlying reason a problem happens
Fixing it prevents repeats.
w: The first person who noticed the problem
The most visible symptom of the problem
The cost of fixing the problem once

q: A store keeps getting damaged shipments. Replacing items each time does not stop it. What should it do?
r: Find and fix the cause, such as poor packing or rough handling
Fixing the root cause prevents repeats.
w: Keep replacing items forever without checking why

q: What is a quality audit?
r: A review that checks whether quality procedures are followed
It identifies gaps.
w: A review of how much tax a company owes
A review of employees' vacation days

q: What is a warranty claim a sign of?
r: A possible quality problem with a product
Claims suggest products failed.
w: A growing market for a new product
A fall in the product's price

q: Warranty claims for one model jump 40 percent in a month. What should management do?
r: Investigate the cause and take corrective action
The rise signals a possible defect.
w: Ignore the increase because sales are up
Remove all warranties from the product
Raise the price of the model immediately
That does not address the cause.

q: What is a service quality gap?
r: The difference between what customers expect and what they receive
Closing it raises satisfaction.
w: The difference between a firm's cost and its price
The difference between two competing products' prices
The difference between a firm's sales and its goals

q: A hotel promises quiet rooms but guests report noisy hallways. What is this?
r: A service quality gap
Expectations were not met.

q: What does zero defects mean as a goal?
r: Striving to make every product right the first time
It sets a very high standard.
w: Accepting any number of defects as normal
Producing nothing so that no defects occur

q: What is just-in-time (JIT) production?
r: Making goods only as they are needed to reduce waste
It lowers inventory costs.
w: Making large amounts of goods far ahead of orders
Making goods only once each year

q: Which is a risk of just-in-time production?
r: A supply delay can halt production because there is little stock
Low inventory leaves little buffer.
w: Having too much unsold inventory in storage
Paying high storage costs for huge stockpiles

q: What is customer satisfaction?
r: How well a product or service meets or exceeds expectations
Satisfied customers return.
w: The number of products a company makes each day
The price a customer pays for a product
The number of stores a company owns

q: Which action best raises customer satisfaction?
r: Listening to feedback and fixing recurring problems
It addresses what customers want.

q: What is risk?
r: The chance that something will cause loss or harm
Businesses face many kinds of risk.
w: A certain outcome that cannot be avoided
A reward for taking a good decision

q: What is risk management?
r: Identifying, assessing and reducing risks
It protects a business from loss.
w: Ignoring risks until a loss occurs
Taking as many risks as possible

q: What are the four basic ways to handle risk?
r: Avoid, reduce, transfer or accept it
Each response fits different situations.
w: Ignore, hide, delay or deny it
Buy, sell, trade or lend it
Print, store, mail or recycle it

q: What is risk avoidance?
r: Choosing not to do an activity that carries a risk
It removes the exposure.
w: Buying insurance to cover a loss
Taking steps to lower the chance of a loss
Accepting the risk and planning to cover losses

q: What is risk transfer?
r: Shifting the financial burden of a risk to another party
Insurance is a common example.
w: Accepting the loss as a cost of business
Lowering the chance of the loss with safety steps

q: What is risk reduction?
r: Taking steps to lower the chance or impact of a loss
Safety training and alarms are examples.

q: A shop installs security cameras and alarms to prevent theft. Which strategy is this?
r: Risk reduction
The steps lower the chance of loss.

q: A company buys fire insurance for its warehouse. Which strategy is this?
r: Risk transfer
The insurer takes on the cost.
w: The company is not paying alone.

q: A company decides not to expand into a country with unstable politics. Which strategy is this?
r: Risk avoidance
It chooses not to enter the risky activity.
w: The activity is not being done safer.
The company is not taking the risk.

q: What is insurance?
r: A contract that pays for certain losses in exchange for premiums
It spreads risk across many policyholders.
w: A loan that must be repaid with interest
A savings plan that earns interest
A tax paid on risky activities

q: What is a premium?
r: The amount paid for an insurance policy
It may be paid monthly or yearly.
w: The amount the insurer pays after a loss
The amount owed before coverage starts
The profit that an insurer makes

q: What is a deductible?
r: The amount the policyholder pays before insurance pays
Higher deductibles lower premiums.
w: The monthly cost of a policy
The most the insurer will pay
A refund given for no claims

q: A policy has a $1,000 deductible and a loss of $4,500 is covered. How much does the insurer pay?
What is liability insurance?
r: Coverage for harm or damage a business causes to others
It protects against lawsuits.
w: Coverage for a business's own property only

q: What is property insurance?
r: Coverage for loss or damage to a business's own buildings and goods
It covers fire, theft and storms.
w: Coverage for harm caused to customers
Coverage for a loan that is not repaid

q: What is workers' compensation insurance?
r: Coverage for employees injured on the job
It pays medical costs and lost wages.

q: What is a hazard?
r: A condition that may cause harm or loss
Wet floors are an example.
w: A rule that employees must follow

q: A wet floor with no sign is an example of a:
r: Hazard
It can cause a fall.

q: What is a risk assessment?
r: A review that identifies risks and judges how likely and serious they are
It guides what to do first.
w: A list of customers who might not pay
A forecast of next year's profits

q: Which risk should be addressed first?
r: One that is both likely and very costly
High likelihood and impact need attention.
w: One that is unlikely and very cheap
One that has already been fixed
One that no one has ever noticed

q: What is a contingency plan?
r: A plan for what to do if something goes wrong
It prepares a business for emergencies.
w: A plan to increase prices next year
A plan to hire more employees
A plan to open a new store

q: A restaurant keeps a backup generator in case of power loss. What is this?
r: A contingency measure
It prepares for a possible outage.

q: Why does a business keep emergency funds?
r: To cover unexpected costs without borrowing
Reserves provide a cushion.
w: To pay for yearly advertising only

q: What is fraud?
r: Intentional deception to gain something unfairly
It can cause serious losses.
w: An honest mistake in a calculation
A late payment to a supplier

q: Which control best reduces the risk of employee theft of cash?
r: Separating duties so no one person handles cash from start to finish
Checks and balances reduce fraud.
w: Letting one person handle all cash with no review
Keeping cash in an unlocked drawer

q: What is cybersecurity risk?
r: The chance of loss from attacks on computer systems and data
Hackers and malware are threats.
w: The chance of a product being returned
The chance of staff arriving late

q: Which practice most reduces the risk of a phishing attack?
r: Training employees to spot and report suspicious emails
Awareness lowers the chance of a breach.
w: Encouraging staff to click every link

q: What is financial risk?
r: The chance that a business will lose money or be unable to pay debts
Debt and cash shortages create it.
w: The chance that products will be stolen
The chance that employees will resign
The chance that a store will be remodeled

q: A firm borrows heavily to expand and sales fall. What risk has increased?
r: Financial risk
Debt payments continue when sales fall.

q: What is a safety data sheet (SDS)?
r: A document that explains hazards and safe handling of a chemical
Workers use it to stay safe.
w: A sheet that lists employees' pay
A sheet that shows product prices

q: An employee must clean with a chemical they do not know. What should they do first?
r: Read the safety data sheet and follow the instructions
It explains hazards and protection.
w: Use it without looking at any instructions
Mix it with other cleaners to test it
Ask a customer what to do

q: What does OSHA do?
r: Sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards
Employers must follow its rules.
w: Licenses all businesses in a state
